opus-5.5.text:
I think the deeper purpose isn't really the hardware itself. When people see a new dexterous hand or a more agile humanoid, it's easy to get excited about the mechanics: more degrees of freedom, better torque density, finer tactile sensing. But for me, the real value of better hardware is that it widens the space of things a robot *can* experience, and that ultimately determines what it can learn.

Look at how intelligence developed in language models. The breakthrough came from data: an enormous, diverse record of human expression. Robotics doesn't have that yet. We don't have an internet-scale corpus of physical interaction. So in a sense, hardware is the "data collection device" for embodied intelligence. If a robot can only grip and place, the data it produces is narrow, and the model trained on it will be narrow too. If the hardware lets it fold cloth, twist a lid, handle something fragile, or recover when it slips, then every one of those interactions becomes a learning signal about how the physical world behaves.

So I'd frame it this way: hardware sets the ceiling on what kind of world the robot gets to touch, and the model determines how much it can understand from that contact. The two have to co-evolve. Very capable hardware without a good learning framework is just an expensive puppet. A powerful model without capable hardware is stuck in simulation, or limited to tasks that don't really matter in people's lives.

There's also a practical side. The more tasks a single robot can do, the more justifiable it is to deploy at scale. Once you deploy at scale, you get a flywheel: more robots in real environments, more real-world data, better models, which in turn make the hardware more useful. Much of the hardware progress we're seeing now is really about getting that flywheel to start turning.

So the deeper purpose, I'd say, is giving intelligence a body rich enough that it can actually learn about the world, not just move around in it.

r001.rationale: The response says better hardware lets robots experience more interactions, and that each interaction becomes a learning signal for models to understand the physical world.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the deeper purpose is actually not about the hardware itself. When people see a new robot that can pour water or fold clothes, the natural reaction is to ask what the robot can do now. But for me, the more interesting question is what the robot can learn now.

Every time hardware improves, it changes what kind of data you can collect and what kind of interaction becomes possible. A hand with better tactile sensing is not just a hand that grasps more objects. It is a channel through which the model can experience contact, slip, pressure, all these things that you simply cannot get from a video on the internet. So hardware developments expand the boundary of what the model is allowed to perceive and try. That is the real value.

I come from the generative model side, and in that world we have seen this pattern again and again. The breakthrough is rarely one clever idea. It is usually that the data finally covers the space you care about, and then the model does the rest. Robotics has been stuck partly because the physical world is expensive to sample. You cannot scrape the real world. So better actuators, cheaper sensors, more durable bodies, these are really tools for making physical experience cheaper to collect, more diverse, and safer to collect at scale.

There is another layer too. Humans and robots need to share the same environment. Our homes, our kitchens, our offices were designed for human bodies. If the hardware can approach human form factor and human level dexterity, then the robot does not need the world to be rebuilt for it. It can learn from humans directly, imitate humans directly, and eventually the gap between human demonstration and robot execution becomes small enough that learning transfers.

So when I think about hardware, I do not think "more tasks" is the goal. More tasks is a symptom. The purpose is to give an embodied intelligence a body that is rich enough and general enough that learning itself can become the engine, instead of engineers handcrafting each capability one at a time. Once that happens, the number of tasks stops being something we count. It becomes something that grows on its own.

r001.rationale: The response says hardware expands what models can perceive and experience, making richer physical data available so they can learn; performing more tasks is described as a symptom of that learning.

astra-6.text: I think the deeper purpose is to expand what people can do. Enabling a robot to perform more tasks is an important technical step, but the real value comes when those capabilities help someone in everyday life—by taking on dangerous work, reducing repetitive labor, or helping a person live more independently. So hardware development should ultimately serve human needs. The question is not just whether a robot can do something, but whether it can do it reliably and affordably enough to make someone’s life better.

r001.rationale: The response frames hardware advances as a way to help people and improve daily life. It does not say that enabling robots to perform more tasks helps models learn more knowledge.

sol-6.1.text: I think the deeper purpose is to expand what people are able to do. Better hardware lets robots take on more of the physical work that is dangerous, exhausting, or repetitive, giving people more time and freedom to focus on things they value. So performing more tasks is a means to an end. The real question is whether those capabilities translate into useful, accessible help in everyday life.

r001.rationale: The response frames broader task capability as a way to expand what people can do and provide useful help; it does not say hardware development enables models to learn more knowledge.
